sessions.title: One minute to breathe
script: Stop. Right where you are, exactly as you are.
Standing, sitting, in a hallway: anywhere works. Eyes open is fine.
Breathe in gently through your nose… two… three… four.
And let the air out even more slowly, as if through a straw… two… three… four… five… six.
Now, observe. Three quick questions, one word each.
Your body: what stands out? Tight, hot, tired… Just one word.
Your emotion: irritation, worry, nothing much? One word, no judgment.
Your mind: what is it busy with, right now? One more word.
[pause 3s]
Simply naming it already gives you a step back.
A second slow breath. In… two… three… four. And out, no rush, all the way to the end.
And now, proceed. What's the next small thing to do? Not the whole day. Just the very next step.
Picking up that call. Opening that door. Answering that one message.
Got it? Go, with this calmer breath.

sessions.title: Box breathing
script: Sit or stand tall, feet flat, shoulders settled. Here we go.
Box breathing has four sides, four counts each.
Firefighters, nurses and pilots use it to keep a clear head when the pressure is on.
You breathe in for four, hold for four, breathe out for four, then rest with empty lungs for four.
All through the nose, without straining, like tracing a square in your mind. One side goes up, one runs flat across, one comes down, one runs back.
I'll count for you. Start by gently letting your air out.
[pause 2s]
Breathe in… two… three… four.
Hold… two… three… four.
Breathe out… two… three… four.
Empty… two… three… four.
Again. Breathe in… two… three… four.
Hold, with your throat soft… two… three… four.
Breathe out… two… three… four.
Wait… two… three… four.
One last round together. Breathe in… two… three… four.
Hold, shoulders staying loose… two… three… four.
Breathe out, shoulders dropping… two… three… four.
Wait, nice and easy… two… three… four.
Now I'll count less. Keep the same square, and I'll just call out the corners.
In… and four.
Hold… and four.
Out… and four.
Wait… and four.
If holding for four feels uncomfortable, shrink it to three. A smaller square is still a square.
Feeling dizzy or uneasy? Simply go back to your natural breath.
One more round, more quietly. In… hold… out… wait.
While you're counting, your mind is busy. There's less room left for whatever was worrying you.
[pause 4s]
Notice the four corners: the top of the breath, the bottom of the breath, and those little plateaus in between, where everything is still.
One last square, all your own, at your own pace.
Then let the counting fade. Your breath returns to its natural shape, on its own.
You've found your footing again, with a slightly clearer mind. You can head back in now.

sessions.title: Stressed in public, discreetly
script: No one around you will notice a thing. Keep your eyes open, stay as you are.
Everything we're about to do is invisible. From the outside, you simply look like you're waiting.
Start with your feet. Standing or seated, press them lightly into the floor, as if to push it down a millimeter.
Feel the pressure under your heels, then under the balls of your feet. The ground pushes back. It's holding you up.
Release, then press again, gently.
That simple contact reminds your body that it's standing somewhere real, here and now.
[pause 3s]
Move to your hands. They can stay in your pockets, on your lap, or wrapped around a rail.
Press the tip of your thumb against your index finger. A small, firm squeeze, for two seconds.
Then against your middle finger. Then your ring finger. Then your little finger.
And back the other way, feeling each contact: the warmth, the texture of the skin, the fingernail under your thumb.
If your thoughts are racing, this gives them a rhythm to follow. One finger, then the next.
Now let your gaze rest on something neutral. A coat button, the corner of a poster, a mark on the floor.
No need to stare. Let your eyes rest there, as if looking out of a train window.
Your field of vision can widen a little at the edges. Your brow softens.
[pause 3s]
Now, the breath. Mouth closed, no one hears you breathing.
Breathe in easily through your nose, without lifting your chest… two… three.
And let the exhale last a little longer. The air slides out through your nostrils, slowly, silently… four… five… six.
Once more. An ordinary breath in… and a breath out that takes its time.
At the end of the exhale, your shoulders drop by half an inch. Invisible to everyone else, but not to you.
A longer exhale gently tells your body it can slow down.
Keep this quiet rhythm while you listen around you.
Pick out a first sound. The hum of an engine, a distant voice, the clicking of a keyboard.
Don't judge it. Just notice it.
Then a second one, closer. Footsteps, the rustle of a jacket.
And a third, quieter one. One you only hear when you listen closely.
[pause 3s]
Three sounds, and here you are, in this place, rather than inside a busy head.
The noise and the crowd haven't changed. But you've found your anchors again: your feet, your fingers, your gaze, your breath.
You can do this anywhere. In a line, in a meeting, in a packed elevator.
Even thirty seconds can already help. A press of the feet, a round of the fingers, one long exhale.
Go back to what you were doing, at your own pace. Your anchor travels with you.

sessions.title: Quick reset
script: You did the right thing by pressing pause. The next three minutes are for you.
Place both feet flat on the floor. Feel your heels, then the whole soles of your feet.
Let your back lengthen, as if a thread were gently drawing your head upward.
We're going to use a very simple tool: the double sigh.
Your body already knows it. It does it on its own, after a good cry, or just before sleep.
Two breaths in through the nose, one right after the other: a big one, then a small top-up.
Then a very long breath out through the mouth, all the way to the end. It's that long exhale that can help your body release the pressure.
If you feel lightheaded at any point, simply go back to your usual breathing.
[pause 2s]
First sigh. Breathe in through your nose, deeply…
and add one small sip of air on top.
Now breathe out through your mouth, slowly, like a balloon letting go of its air… three… four… five… six… seven… eight.
Notice your shoulders. During that exhale, they may already have started to drop.
Second sigh. A big breath in through the nose… and a little more.
And let it all go through the mouth. Your shoulders slide down, away from your ears… five… six… seven… eight.
You might feel a little warmth, or a tingle in your hands. That's often a sign your body is unwinding.
Last sigh. Breathe in… and a little more, right at the top.
Let it out, long and slow. Let the weight of your arms draw your shoulders toward the floor… five… six… seven… eight.
[pause 3s]
Now, your jaw. That's often where stress hides without us noticing it.
Let your teeth part by a few millimeters. Your lips can stay closed.
Rest your tongue flat behind your lower teeth, completely soft.
Your cheeks relax, and the space between your eyebrows widens. Even your eyes can rest.
Now let your breath do whatever it wants. You're not steering it anymore.
Feel what's supporting your body: your feet on the floor, your hips on the seat, or the weight sinking down through your legs if you're standing.
Everything that's holding you up. Lean into it for a moment; let the ground do some of the work.
[pause 4s]
Maybe something has shifted. A little more room in your chest. Or nothing in particular, and that's fine too.
The double sigh goes everywhere with you. Just one, in the middle of a meeting or out on the street, can already help. No one needs to notice.
Now come back to your day. Not to everything that's left to do. Just to the next step.
Then the one after that. One step at a time.

sessions.title: When anger rises
script: Anger has just surged up in you. A word, an email, a situation that crossed a line.
It's allowed to be here. Often, it's a sign that something important to you has been touched.
We're not going to make it disappear. We're only going to take care of what you do with it in the next few minutes.
[pause 3s]
First, find where it's burning in your body.
Maybe in your jaw, clenched, teeth pressed together.
Maybe in your fists, or in your forearms, ready to spring.
Or in your chest: heat, pressure, a pounding heart.
Sometimes it's a knot in the stomach, or a face that's burning.
You don't need to change anything yet. Just notice the hottest spot. Simply locating it already gives you back a little control.
Now, your hands. If they're clenched, open them slowly, one finger at a time.
Rest them on your thighs, palms facing up, or let them hang loosely by your sides.
Feel the air on the inside of your hands. Open hands are not the same as clenched fists. Your body notices the difference.
[pause 3s]
Let's cool things down a little with the breath.
Breathe in through your nose, normally.
Then blow out slowly through your mouth, lips slightly rounded, as if you were cooling a spoonful of soup that's far too hot.
Not hard: just a thin stream of air, long and steady… four… five… six.
Again. Breathe in easily… and blow on the soup, nice and long… four… five… six… seven.
A third time. Notice the end of the exhale, that little moment when the air is out and nothing is urgent.
The long exhale is like your body's brake pedal. Every slow breath out presses on it a little more.
Keep this rhythm going while you take a closer look at the anger.
Behind it, there's almost always a need. Something that matters to you and wasn't respected.
Maybe respect: someone spoke to you in a way that isn't okay with you.
Maybe fairness: what happened feels unjust.
Maybe rest: you're running on empty, and this was the last straw.
Or something else: being heard, being recognized, feeling safe.
Look for the word that feels right to you. Say it silently to yourself, once or twice.
[pause 3s]
Naming that need doesn't mean your anger is wrong. It helps you see what you actually want to protect.
Take another long exhale, like blowing on the soup. Feel your shoulders come down a notch, and your jaw loosen a little.
Now you have a choice. And that choice belongs to you.
You can respond now, if you feel calm enough to say what matters without hurting anyone.
You can respond later. In an hour, tomorrow, after a walk or a night's sleep. Nothing forces you to react in the heat of the moment.
If it's an email, you can even write your reply without sending it, and reread it once you've cooled down.
You can also decide not to respond at all, if it isn't worth it.
All three options are valid. Let the one that feels most right, here and now, come to you.
Notice what your body says about it. Often, the right option is the one that lets you breathe a little more freely.
[pause 3s]
Before you carry on, one last breath. In through the nose… two… three… four.
And blow out long and slow, keeping your hands open… four… five… six… seven.
The anger may still be there, a little less fierce. That's normal: it tends to come down in stages.
You know what you need, and you know you get to choose your response.
You can go back to your day now, in your own way.

sessions.title: Too much at once
script: It's a lot. Too many things at once, and everything feels urgent.
Feeling overwhelmed like this is normal. It's not a lack of ability. It's just too much for one head at once.
For four minutes, set it all down. None of it will fly away.
[pause 3s]
Start with three long exhales.
Breathe in through your nose, without forcing. Then blow out through your mouth, slowly, emptying fully… four… five… six.
Second one. The air comes in… and goes out, more slowly than usual… five… six… seven.
Third one. Let the exhale carry away a little of the tension in your forehead and shoulders, all the way to the end.
When everything speeds up, slowing your breath is one of the few things you can do right away.
Now, feel your hands. Rest them flat on a table, on your thighs, or one inside the other.
Notice their weight, their temperature. Are your fingers cold, warm, a little numb?
Also pick a fixed point in front of you: a corner of the wall, a door handle, an object on your desk.
Let your gaze rest there. It no longer needs to jump between screens.
[pause 3s]
Hands resting, eyes resting. You have something steady to lean on.
Your body doesn't need to rush in every direction for things to move forward. For now, it can stay here.
Now let's empty your head. Not to organize, just to let out what's spinning.
Silently name everything that's on your mind, in any order, without sorting. A word or two for each thing.
The report that's due. The unanswered message. The groceries. That appointment. That conversation that keeps nagging at you.
Let your own things come, big and tiny alike. Each one gets its name, just once.
You can even count them discreetly on your fingers.
Work. Home. The people waiting for an answer. The things you're worried about for later. Anything can come up.
[pause 3s]
If more keep coming, keep going. You don't have to do anything with these thoughts right now, except acknowledge them.
Notice: once they're named, they often take up a little less space. They're still there, but they're no longer all shouting at once.
Your mind was trying to hold everything in memory at the same time. Now that it's all been named, it can loosen its grip a little.
Take one long exhale… four… five… six.
Now, just one question. Out of all of that, what's the one thing that really matters in the next hour?
Not necessarily the biggest, or the most urgent to others. The one that would bring you the most relief once it's done. Or the one that truly can't wait.
Let the answer come. If you're torn between two, choose the simpler one. You can change it later.
[pause 3s]
You've got your one thing. Now picture the very first small step to get started on it.
Really small. Opening the document. Writing the first line of the email. Finding the number in your phone.
See yourself doing it. Where are your hands? What do you see on the screen, or in front of you?
Feel how doable that one step is, even now, even tired.
One small, clear step is often what gets everything else moving again.
The rest of the list hasn't disappeared. It's waiting its turn. And it will get it, one thing after another.
You don't have to carry it all at once. Just this one step. When it's done, you'll choose the next one, in the same way.
One last long exhale, hands resting, eyes on your fixed point.
And now, go and take that first step. Everything else can wait its turn.

sessions.title: Panic anchor
script: I'm here with you. Keep your eyes open.
What you're feeling is very unpleasant. And it isn't dangerous. It will pass.
Even if it feels huge right now, a wave like this always comes back down.
Place both feet flat on the floor. If there's a seat under you, feel that too. If you're standing, bend your knees very slightly.
Press down through your heels. The floor is solid. It isn't moving. It holds you, whatever your body is doing.
Now press your hands together, palm against palm, in front of your chest or on your knees.
Push firmly for a few seconds. Feel the strength in your arms, the warmth between your palms.
[pause 3s]
And release. Keep your hands together, more gently now. Your feet, your hands: you have anchors.
Look around you. Let your eyes wander slowly around the room or street.
Choose an object and name it, under your breath if you can. Just its name. A chair. A window. A bag.
A second object. Notice its color as you name it.
And a third. Take your time. There's no right answer.
Naming what you see helps your attention come back here, to this place, instead of the alarm.
[pause 3s]
Now, the breath. You don't need to take a big breath in. Let the air come in however it comes.
And blow out through your mouth, slowly, as if onto a candle you don't want to put out… three… four… five.
Again. The air comes in on its own… and you let it flow out for a long time, through your mouth… three… four… five… six.
It's the exhale that matters. The inhale takes care of itself. You don't have to reach for it.
Feeling short of air is very common in moments like this. You are breathing, and the air is moving.
Another exhale, soft and long, like a thin stream of air over the flame.
Now imagine a wave. It rises, it swells, it can seem very high.
Then it reaches its peak. And, like every wave, it starts to come back down.
What you're going through follows the same movement. You may be at the top, or already on the way down.
You don't have to stop the wave. You only have to stay on your feet while it passes.
[pause 3s]
The sensations may still be there. A racing heart. Heat, tingling, a tight throat.
These are your body's alarm signals. They're loud, and they aren't dangerous. They rise, and then they settle down on their own.
You don't need to fight them. Let them be there, beside you, while you keep breathing out long and slow.
Come back to your feet. Press down into the floor a little.
Your hands, still together. You can press a little harder if it helps you come back here.
One object in front of you. Name it once more. And one long exhale, through your mouth.
You're still here. You're getting through it, one exhale at a time.
Notice, even slightly, whether anything has changed. Your breath a little less short. Your shoulders a little lower. Or not yet, and that's okay too.
[pause 3s]
You've made it through this wave. That takes a lot of energy. You can stay seated a while longer, have a glass of water, take it slowly.
Feeling tired afterward, with legs a bit wobbly, is common. Your body gave a lot, and now it's recovering.
If these attacks come back often, talk to a doctor or a health professional. Real help exists, and no one should have to handle this without support.
For now, one last long exhale. And move on at your own pace, feet firmly on the ground.

sessions.title: Lower your cortisol
script: For five minutes, you'll learn a rhythm. The simplest and most useful one in CortiFree: a short breath in, a long breath out.
Sit on a chair or lie on your back, as you prefer. Let your shoulders drop.
Place one hand on your belly, just below your navel. The other can rest on your thigh, or on your chest.
You can close your eyes, or let your gaze rest on the floor ahead of you.
[pause 3s]
Before we start, one simple idea.
Your body has two main modes. An alert mode, which speeds everything up so you can cope. And a recovery mode, which slows down, digests, and repairs.
When you breathe in, your heart speeds up very slightly. When you breathe out, it slows down a little. It happens naturally, with every breath.
So lengthening your exhale means spending more time on the slowing side. Many people feel it helps their body shift toward recovery.
It isn't magic, and there's nothing to get right. It's a signal you can send your body, again and again: you are safe.
Start by noticing your breath just as it is. Without changing it.
Under your hand, your belly rises a little as you breathe in, and falls as you breathe out. Or maybe it's mostly your chest that moves. Both are normal.
Notice whether your breath is short or deep, fast or slow. Just take note.
Notice the air, too: cooler coming in, warmer going out.
It doesn't need to be calm already. We start from wherever you are.
And notice the small natural pause right at the bottom of the exhale, just before the air comes back. We'll learn to stretch it a little.
[pause 3s]
Now let's move into the rhythm. Breathe in through your nose for four counts, and out through your mouth or nose for six.
I'll count with you.
Breathe in… two… three… four.
Breathe out… two… three… four… five… six.
Breathe in, your belly rising under your hand… three… four.
Breathe out, slowly… two… three… four… five… six.
Again. Breathe in… two… three… four.
And let it go, as if you were blowing on a candle without making the flame flicker… four… five… six.
Breathe in… two… three… four.
Breathe out… two… three… four… five… six.
I'll count more softly now. Keep the same rhythm. Four to come in, six to go out.
In… and four.
Out… slowly… and six.
If your mind wanders off, that's normal. Come back to the count, without blaming yourself. Every return is part of the practice.
[pause 3s]
If it's comfortable, lengthen the exhale further. Seven counts, or eight.
Keep the inhale at four. Only the breath out stretches.
Picture the air flowing out like a thin stream of water, fine and steady, down to the very last drop.
Breathe in… two… three… four.
Breathe out… two… three… four… five… six… seven… eight.
If eight is too much, stay at six or seven. The right rhythm never leaves you gasping for the next breath.
Breathe in… two… three… four.
Breathe out, ever so gently… three… four… five… six… seven… eight.
Breathe in… two… three… four.
And the stream of water flows on… four… five… six… seven… eight.
Feeling dizzy or uncomfortable? Simply return to your natural breath. There's no hurry.
[pause 3s]
Now let the counting go. The numbers fade away, but keep the slowness.
An easy breath in. A longer breath out, taking all the time it needs.
Under your hand, feel your belly rise… then fall, slowly.
If you lose the rhythm, simply take one longer exhale. It puts you back on track.
With each exhale, something can settle. Your forehead widens. Your jaw loosens. Your shoulders slide a little lower.
Your hands may grow a little heavier, a little warmer. Let it happen.
There's nothing to make happen. You're simply giving your body time to follow.
[pause 3s]
Notice what has changed since the beginning, if anything.
Maybe a slower breath. Warmer hands. A little more space in your chest. Or simply the feeling of being a bit more here.
And if you notice nothing in particular, that's fine too. The signal has been sent.
Let your breathing return to its natural pace. Your hand can leave your belly.
This rhythm is yours now. Four to breathe in, six to breathe out. No one can see it.
You can use it in a line, before a meeting, on your commute, in bed at night. Three breaths are enough to get started.
Gently move your fingers, your shoulders. And whenever it feels right for you, open your eyes.

sessions.title: After an argument
script: An argument has just happened. With someone who matters to you, and that's exactly why it's so unsettling.
You don't have to sort anything out in the next few minutes. Just come back down, and see things a little more clearly.
Settle in wherever you are. On a chair, standing against a wall, it doesn't matter. If you need to change rooms, now is a good time.
[pause 3s]
Start by noticing what's happening inside you, without changing anything.
Your heart may be beating faster, or harder. You can feel it in your chest, in your throat, sometimes even in your temples.
There may be some heat. In your face, at the back of your neck, in your hands.
And in your head, the scene is probably replaying. The words that were said, the tone, that look.
Your hands may be trembling a little, too. A lump in your throat, an urge to cry or to shout.
All of this is normal. It's your body still on alert, ready to defend itself. It needs a little time to realize the tense moment is over.
Let's help it along with a few long exhales.
Breathe in through your nose, simply… two… three… four. Then blow out through your mouth, slowly, a little longer than the inhale… four… five… six.
Again. And as the air leaves, let your shoulders drop. They may have crept up toward your ears during the argument.
A third time. The air goes out, your shoulders come down another notch, your hands unclench.
A fourth one, even slower. Feel your belly soften at the end of the exhale.
Keep breathing like this, at your own pace, with an exhale that takes its time.
Comebacks will probably keep popping up. “I should have told them…” “Next time, I'll say…”
That's what the mind does after a conflict: it hunts for the perfect line, it replays the match.
You don't need to follow these comebacks, or push them away. Just notice them, the way you'd watch cars go by from the sidewalk.
Oh, there's one. It passes. And you come back to your exhale.
You can even label it with one word: “replaying.” And come back to your breath.
Every time you return to the breath, you give your body a little more time to settle down.
If one line keeps coming back again and again, you can answer it silently: “I hear you. Not now.”
[pause 3s]
Now turn toward yourself. Not toward what the other person did, but toward what's happening inside you.
What are you feeling, right now, underneath the agitation? Maybe sadness. Hurt. Fear. Exhaustion. Sometimes several at once.
Put a word to it, the one that feels true.
Notice where it sits in your body: your throat, your chest, your belly. You can rest a hand there, if that helps.
And behind that feeling, what do you need? To be heard? Respected? Some calm? Recognition for everything you do?
That need is legitimate. It doesn't make you difficult. It simply tells you what matters to you.
[pause 3s]
Take a long exhale, and let that need stay where it is, acknowledged.
Now, if you feel up to it, take a small step to the side. Picture the scene from the other person's place.
Not to say they were right. Just to see a slightly bigger picture.
What might this person have been feeling during the argument? Frustration? Worry? Feeling like they didn't matter?
And what do they need, on their side?
Often we find that the two needs aren't so opposed after all. Two people who each wanted, in their own way, to feel respected or reassured.
You don't have to guess right. A best guess is enough.
And if it's too soon to put yourself in their shoes, that's okay. You can come back to it later.
[pause 3s]
Breathe. An easy breath in… and a long breath out, gently emptying.
Now picture the moment when you reconnect. Later on, when the time is right.
What could your first sentence be? A calm one, that opens things up instead of starting the fight again.
Maybe: “I don't like how things went earlier.” Or: “I'd like us to talk about it again, more calmly.” Or simply: “I care about you, even when we disagree.”
Choose your own, in your own words. One sentence is enough to begin.
A sentence about you, about what you feel and what you need, is often easier to hear than a reproach.
Say it to yourself silently, slowly, and notice what it does in your body.
[pause 3s]
And nothing says you have to fix everything right away.
Sometimes it takes a few hours, or a night, for both of you to come back down. That delay isn't a failure. It's often what makes a real conversation possible.
Take one more long exhale. Feel your feet on the floor, the weight of your body, your back straightening a little.
Notice where you are now, compared to the beginning. Maybe a slightly slower heart, a slightly less crowded head. Or still some agitation, and that's okay.
[pause 3s]
You've made some space between the argument and whatever comes next. That space is what will let you choose your words.
Go back to your day, gently, with your sentence in your pocket for the right moment, whenever it comes.

sessions.title: After bad news
script: Something hard has just happened. A call, a message, an announcement.
You don't have to understand or decide anything right now. Just take this time for yourself.
If you can, sit down. Or lean your back against a wall.
If you're outside, find a bench, a low wall, a quieter corner. Put your phone down if you can, screen facing the table or tucked in your pocket.
[pause 3s]
Start by looking around you. Slowly, let your eyes travel around the room you're in.
The walls, their color. A window, the light coming in. A piece of furniture, a familiar object.
Let your eyes rest on three things, one after another, without hurrying.
Name them silently, simply. “The lamp. The door. My mug.” It helps your mind remember where you are.
After a shock, everything can feel unreal. Looking at what surrounds you is a gentle way back into the present.
Now feel the floor beneath your feet. It's there, steady. Feel the seat holding you, the backrest behind you.
You're here, in this room. What just happened is real. And you are here too.
Both are true at the same time: the news, and this floor holding you up.
Notice the temperature of the air on your hands, on your face. The touch of your clothes. These small, ordinary things are still here.
[pause 3s]
Let your breathing slow down a little, if it's willing. There's no goal, no counting.
Just a breath in, whenever it comes. And a breath out, a little longer, if that's possible.
Another one. The air comes in however it can… and goes out, effortlessly, without trying to do it right.
If your breath stays short or ragged, that's okay too. Your body is reacting to something big. You don't have to correct it.
If you like, press your feet a little more firmly into the floor, and let the exhale leave through your mouth, like a sigh.
[pause 3s]
Whatever you're feeling right now, it's normal.
Maybe a kind of numbness, as if everything were wrapped in cotton wool, with no clear thoughts. That's a very common reaction to shock.
Maybe tears are rising. You can let them come. They belong here.
Maybe anger, disbelief, an urge to run away.
Or thoughts racing in every direction: what if, what now, how will I cope. You don't have to answer them yet.
Or maybe nothing at all, for now. A big blank. That happens too, and it doesn't mean this doesn't matter.
There's no right way to react. All of these reactions are ways for your body to absorb the blow.
And they may shift through the day, coming and going in waves. That's normal too.
You don't have to choose how to feel. Just let whatever is here exist, for the length of this pause.
If you'd like, place a hand on your heart. Or on your belly. Wherever feels most right.
Feel the warmth of your hand, its gentle weight. Like the hand of a friend resting on you.
And say to yourself, softly: “This is hard, what's happening to me. I'm here for myself.”
Or another phrase that speaks to you more. “I'll take this one step at a time.” “It's okay for this to hurt.”
[pause 3s]
Keep your hand there a little longer, if it feels good. Breathe beneath it.
Feel your chest or belly moving softly under your palm. You're keeping yourself company.
This gesture may seem very small. Yet many people find it soothes a little, like having someone there.
Now, just one question. Not for tomorrow, not for the week. Only for the next hour.
What do I need, in the next hour?
Maybe a glass of water. Something to eat. Some fresh air. Lying down. Letting someone know you won't be able to do what was planned.
Choose just one thing. Simple, concrete, doable.
Just one, not a list. The rest will come later.
This isn't a small detail. Looking after your body now is what will help you face what comes next.
[pause 3s]
Think of a person, too. Someone you could call or text, if you need to share some of this weight.
Someone close, a friend, a neighbor. You don't have to explain everything. “Something hard is happening, can you call me?” is enough.
Choose that person now, even if you only reach out later. See their face, hear their voice, just for a moment.
And if no one comes to mind, or if it feels too heavy, support lines exist, and your doctor can be a source of support too.
You don't have to carry this alone. Asking for help isn't a weakness. It's one way of taking care of yourself.
[pause 3s]
Come back to your breath, just as it is now. Feel your feet on the floor again, and the seat beneath you.
You don't need to feel better right away. What happened will take time, and that's normal.
The next few hours may have their ups and downs. You can come back to this pause as many times as you need.
For now, you've done something important: you stopped, and you took care of yourself for a few minutes.
When the moment comes, move toward what you need in the next hour. One thing at a time.

sessions.title: Your inner refuge
script: These seven minutes are for building something you'll keep: an inner refuge. A place where your body feels safe, and where you'll be able to return in a few seconds, even in the middle of a busy day.
Get comfortable, sitting or lying on your back. Let your back be supported, and let your hands rest wherever they feel good.
You can close your eyes, or lower your gaze to a point that isn't moving.
[pause 3s]
Take a slow breath in through your nose… two… three… four.
And let the air leave even more slowly, through your mouth… three… four… five… six.
Once more. The air comes in, cool… and goes out, warm, carrying a little of the day away with it.
One last time. And at the end of the exhale, let your body grow a little heavier, as if it were settling onto whatever is holding it.
[pause 3s]
Now, let a place come to mind where you feel safe.
It can be real: your grandparents' kitchen, a little cove in Brittany, a bench in a park you know by heart. Or completely imaginary: a cabin, a room that exists nowhere else.
Don't look for the perfect place. Take the first one that brings a sense of calm, even a faint one.
If several come up, choose just one for today. And if nothing comes, simply imagine a warm, quiet room, with a door that only opens for you.
If a place brings up difficult memories, set it aside and choose another, more neutral one. This refuge should feel simple and gentle.
[pause 3s]
You're there. Start by looking around.
Which colors stand out? Greens, blues, the warm tones of wood or stone?
And the light: is it morning, late afternoon, the soft glow of a lamp? Where is it coming from? How does it fall on things?
Let your inner gaze wander. Notice a detail close to you: a texture, a shape, an object. Then a detail farther away, on the horizon or at the far end of the room.
You can look up, too. A sky, a ceiling with wooden beams, branches swaying.
The more details you add, the more solid this place becomes. Take your time. If the picture stays blurry, that's fine: some people see very little, and feel a great deal.
[pause 3s]
Now, listen. What can you hear in this place?
Maybe running water, wind in the leaves, waves rolling in. The crackle of a fire, a ticking clock, birds in the distance.
Or a deep, reassuring silence, which has its own texture too.
Notice whether these sounds are near or far, constant or now and then. Let them wrap around you, without any effort.
Breathe in the air of this place. Is there a smell? Cut grass, sea salt, wood, warm bread, clean laundry.
If no smell comes, that's fine. Some places are felt more than they're smelled.
Feel the temperature on your skin. Is the air mild, cool, just the way you like it? Maybe a ray of sunlight on your face, or the warmth of a blanket.
And under your feet, what's there? Sand that gives a little, soft grass, smooth floorboards, a stone warmed by the sun.
Take a few steps, if you like. Feel how the ground responds under each one.
If you sit down in your refuge, feel what's holding you. An armchair, a rock, a soft cushion.
[pause 3s]
Here, nothing is rushing you. No one expects anything from you. There are no notifications, no appointments, no judgment.
Notice how your body responds to this safety. Where do you feel it?
Maybe in your shoulders, letting go. In your belly, unknotting. In your breathing, fuller and slower. In your face, which no longer has to put on a brave front.
Let this feeling spread, like warmth slowly diffusing. You don't have to do anything to keep it. Just notice it.
Take time to really savor it. The more clearly you feel it now, the easier it will be to find it again later.
If part of you stays a little on guard, that's normal. Welcome that part into this place as well. It's allowed to be here.
If a thought from your day comes knocking at the door, that's normal too. You see it, you leave it outside, and you come back to a detail of your refuge: a color, a sound.
[pause 3s]
Now we're going to create a shortcut to this place.
Gently bring the tip of your thumb and index finger together, on one hand or both. A small, discreet circle that no one will notice.
While your fingers are touching, breathe in the calm of your refuge. Its colors. Its sounds. Its temperature. The ease in your body.
As if you were recording all of it into this small gesture.
The gesture and the feeling, together, at the same moment. Breathe in the calm… two… three… four. And let it settle into your fingers… four… five… six.
Release your fingers. Breathe normally.
And make the gesture again. Thumb against index finger. Notice how the refuge comes back, maybe a little faster this time.
A color. A sound. The feeling under your feet. It's all there, in this small circle.
[pause 3s]
The more you repeat this pairing, the more reliable the gesture becomes as a key. At first, it brings back a hint of calm. Over time, it can bring you back here within a few breaths.
Later on, before a meeting, in a waiting room, as you fall asleep, you'll be able to bring these two fingers together and find part of this place again.
You can practice a little each day, when things are going well. That way, the shortcut will be ready on the day you need it.
Now release the gesture. Your refuge stays where it is. It doesn't disappear when you leave it.
You can also return to it simply by closing your eyes, without the gesture, whenever you have a little more time.
Slowly, begin to come back. Feel the support beneath your body, the floor, the chair or the bed.
Hear the sounds of the room you're actually in. The nearest ones first, then those farther away.
Take a slightly fuller breath. Move your fingers and your feet, and stretch if you feel like it.
And whenever it feels right for you, open your eyes. Your shortcut goes with you: thumb to index finger, and your refuge is never far away.
